cards.title: Pre-orders and crowdfunding to fund first manufacturing run
cards.summary: Using a crowdfunding or pre-order campaign to collect cash before paying manufacturing and freight de-risks a first inventory buy.
cards.use_when: You are launching a first product and don't have cash for manufacturing plus freight, and deciding whether to build a pre-order/crowdfunding page before committing to a production run.
steps: Build a simple pre-order or crowdfunding page for the product before paying a factory, and promote it through whatever audience channel you already have (the source case used an existing social audience).

Set the campaign price so total pre-order cash covers at least manufacturing plus the shipping method you will actually use; in the source case, roughly $37,000 raised covered about $9,000 of manufacturing plus air freight.
Collect email addresses from everyone who wants the product but can't buy yet, and use that list as the day-one launch driver when stock arrives.
Expect to convert pre-order buyers manually once inventory lands: the source shipped 700+ pre-order orders by hand before sending the remainder to a fulfillment center.
Treat pre-order demand as a signal for your first inventory quantity, but do not treat it as a substitute for keeping stock available afterward.
caveats: Crowdfunding backers create a delivery obligation and time pressure; the source chose faster air freight partly out of obligation to backers.
Crowdfunding results are a case example, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Customer email list as an Amazon launch accelerator
cards.summary: Building an email list during stockouts lets you concentrate sales and reviews into the first days of an Amazon listing, which the source says improves search ranking.
cards.use_when: You are out of stock, pre-launch, or relaunching an Amazon listing and want to spike early sales velocity to push search rank.
steps: Put an email capture on your own site or social channels offering to notify people when the Amazon listing is live.
Keep collecting during stockouts; the source built this list while waiting months for restock.
On launch day, email the list in one concentrated push so sales and reviews arrive as fast as possible rather than trickling in.
Prioritize getting reviews early, since the source argues early sales plus early reviews signal Amazon to rank the product higher.
Plan inventory for the launch spike: this method concentrates orders and will drain stock quickly.
caveats: The claim that launch velocity causes higher ranking is the source's explanation of Amazon's behavior, not a documented Amazon policy.
Sales ranking returns are described as exponential across positions one through ten, but no specific data is given.

cards.title: Air vs sea freight decision for replenishment
cards.summary: Sea freight costs far less per kilogram but takes weeks; air freight is only justified when being in stock is worth more than the freight premium.
cards.use_when: You are replenishing Amazon inventory and deciding whether to pay for air freight, especially ahead of a peak season or when you are already out of stock.
steps: Get quotes for both options: in the source, sea shipping ran about $2 per kilogram with a 6-week minimum transit, while air shipping ran roughly 5-7 days and cost about $4,200 on one shipment.
Estimate the profit you would lose by being out of stock for the transit delta, and compare it to the air freight premium.
Use air freight when you are facing an out-of-stock during high-demand periods; the source judged one December air shipment worth it because it enabled about $46,000 in December sales.
Split the shipment if the calculation is close: the source's first product used half air and half sea.

Avoid habitual air freight: the source states that unless you really need it, air shipping is largely money thrown away, and one unplanned air shipment cost over $60,000 and consumed most of a month's profit.
caveats: The $2/kg and $4,200 figures are specific quoted examples, not current rates; re-quote every shipment.
The source repeatedly shows that poor inventory planning is the root cause of expensive air freight.

cards.title: Amazon FBA unit economics breakdown for a first product
cards.summary: A worked month-by-month P&L showing that Amazon revenue is reduced by product cost, a 15% referral fee, per-unit pick-and-pack fees, and miscellaneous fees.
cards.use_when: You are pricing a private-label or passion product and need a line-item model of what actually comes out of Amazon revenue.
steps: Start with units times price for gross revenue; the source's first full month was about 1,500 units for just under $55,000.
Subtract cost of goods: about $17,000 in that month, i.e. roughly a third of revenue.
Subtract the Amazon referral fee of 15% of revenue: over $8,000 in that month.
Subtract FBA pick-and-pack fees, charged per unit Amazon ships: over $7,700 in that month, which the source considered worth it versus doing fulfillment himself.
Add back any affiliate commissions if you drive your own traffic through Amazon's affiliate program; the source earned roughly 5% back.
Subtract miscellaneous Amazon fees (about $1,000 that month) and any other business expenses before calling the remainder profit; the result was over $20,000 profit on about $55,000 revenue.

Recalculate landed cost per unit whenever your freight mode changes: the source's landed cost fell from about $11 to about $7.50 per unit after switching from air to sea freight, which protected profit as revenue declined.
caveats: All figures come from one seller's twelve-month case study and are illustrative, not benchmarks.
Referral and FBA fee amounts vary by category, size, weight and current Amazon fee schedules; verify current rates.

cards.title: Judging the 15% Amazon referral fee against paid traffic
cards.summary: The source treats Amazon's 15% referral fee as a substitute for marketing spend, worth paying because the platform supplies buyer traffic.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to sell primarily on Amazon versus your own site, or setting prices that must absorb Amazon's fee.
steps: Compare the 15% referral fee against what you would spend acquiring the same buyer through paid ads on your own store; the source's position is that the fee replaces marketing cost.
If you drive your own traffic to Amazon, reduce the effective fee by routing through your own Amazon affiliate link and earning a commission back (roughly 5% in the source case).
Price products so the referral fee, FBA fees and COGS still leave acceptable margin, rather than treating the fee as the last deduction.

Keep your own store as a parallel channel: in months when the source ran out of Amazon stock, his own website pre-orders did just under $15,000, and later months added $4,000-$20,000 on top of Amazon revenue.
caveats: The 'fee replaces marketing' framing is the source's opinion and assumes you are not also paying for ads.
Affiliate commission rates and program rules change; verify eligibility and current rates.

cards.title: Selling out during a viral spike: redirect demand instead of pausing
cards.summary: When a viral post drains your stock, keep selling through a backup channel rather than letting the demand evaporate.
cards.use_when: Your Amazon inventory hits zero while a social post, press hit, or ad is still driving traffic to the product.
steps: Keep the demand capture alive: the source sent buyers back to his crowdfunding page when his 200 Amazon units sold out in about two hours, doing about $57,000 in one day on that channel.
Do not stop posting content just because inventory is gone; the source continued creating content and later attributed a TV appearance and subsequent sales spikes to that continuous brand building.
Segment buyers by channel: those who will wait pre-order, those who want immediate delivery (send to email list), and those who will buy elsewhere.
Quantify the lost opportunity as a planning input, not a regret: the source estimates he would have sold about $100,000 in one day had Amazon stock been available.
Use this situation as the trigger to increase your next order quantity rather than repeating the stockout.
caveats: The $57,000 day and $100,000 estimate are the seller's own figures from one viral event, not a repeatable result.
Redirecting buyers away from Amazon concentrates revenue on a channel you must fulfill yourself.

cards.title: Building a brand on social media to create compounding product demand
cards.summary: Consistent content around a topic you actually know produces demand spikes and press opportunities that a listing alone won't generate.
cards.use_when: You are planning demand generation for a specialty product and deciding where to invest content effort alongside Amazon SEO.
steps: Pick a product where you have genuine domain knowledge; the source argues content creation is sustainable only when you can speak about the topic from experience (his contrast case was writing about dance without any dance background).
Post continuously, including videos about receiving inventory, packing orders, and the product going live, since these operational moments performed well in the source case.
Accept that content can produce step-change events: the source got an Access Hollywood appearance from a producer who found his social content, which lifted sales for about a week.
Treat a viral post as a demand test and plan inventory accordingly, since the source's 5.7-million-view video emptied 200 units in hours.
Balance both: use Amazon search optimization for shoppers already looking, and social content for shoppers who didn't know the product existed.
caveats: Viral views and TV appearances are outcome examples, not predictable outputs of a content plan.
The source notes that a niche, unique product is what makes an independent website channel viable; commodity products are harder to differentiate this way.

cards.title: Passion-product positioning versus wholesale, arbitrage and private label
cards.summary: The source argues a unique product you are personally invested in outperforms commodity sourcing models and opens extra channels.
cards.use_when: You are choosing which Amazon selling model to pursue, or deciding whether your product is differentiated enough to price above commodity alternatives.
steps: Compare the four models the source names: wholesale, retail arbitrage, private label, and a self-created product; he claims the self-created product works better while acknowledging the others can work.

Test uniqueness by asking whether you could sell the same product on your own website and through specialty retailers; the source's product supported its own site, Etsy, Indiegogo, and wholesale simultaneously.
Check whether your category knowledge lets you produce content, because in the source's framing that content is what generates non-search demand.
If a product is genuinely differentiated, expect channel expansion opportunities (the source got an inbound wholesale order from a retailer who found him on social media).
caveats: 'Passion product beats other models' is the presenter's opinion, not a measured comparison.
Differentiation does not remove the need for good margins, inventory planning, or a quality manufacturer.

cards.title: Diagnosing seasonal demand swings before abandoning a product
cards.summary: A twelve-month view shows predictable slumps and holiday peaks, so judge a product on the year rather than a three-month decline.
cards.use_when: Your Amazon sales are falling for several consecutive months and you are deciding whether to cut the product, hold inventory, or expand channels.
steps: Map revenue by month before reacting: the source's product peaked in December (about $46,000) then fell to about $13,000, $12,000 and $11,000 in the following months.
Check the cause: January followed a stated New Year sobriety trend for a cocktail product, an external seasonal factor rather than a product failure.
Separate revenue decline from margin decline: in the source's low months, profit held up better once cheaper sea freight lowered landed cost from about $11 to about $7.50 per unit.
Use slow periods productively rather than stopping marketing: the source attributes his later recovery partly to continued TikToks, and a slide in output during the slow months weakened the rebound.
Set a review point before you place a large reorder, since the source ordered 7,500 units right before sales dropped and carried the inventory risk through the slump.
caveats: Month-by-month swings in a single case study do not establish a general seasonal pattern for other categories.
Holding inventory through a downturn is a choice with real cash-flow risk; the source describes low bank balances during that period.

cards.title: Diversifying into wholesale when slow Amazon sales leave you overstocked
cards.summary: Sitting on excess inventory is a reason to open wholesale, Etsy and international channels rather than discounting on Amazon.
cards.use_when: You have excess Amazon inventory and stagnant sales and want to move units through other channels.
steps: Convert your site to accept wholesale enquiries and set up a wholesale ordering path, as the source did in his twelfth month, generating over $17,000 in the first push month.
List on additional marketplaces; the source added Etsy and did over $3,000 in a month after being approached by the platform.
Look for inbound wholesale leads from your content, since the source's first wholesale order came from someone who found him on TikTok and wanted the product in their store.
Support reorders: the source highlights a Canadian retailer who sold through quickly and reordered, and was featured in a local magazine for carrying the product.
Take international expansion seriously when it arrives inbound; the source shipped over 3,000 units to Europe and landed a major retailer there.
caveats: Wholesale reduces your per-unit margin versus direct sales.
Channel expansion results in the source case came after sustained social content and a differentiated product, not from listing alone.

cards.title: Freight and freight-driven landed cost as the lever on margin
cards.summary: Switching freight mode can improve margin even when revenue falls, because landed cost per unit drops.
cards.use_when: Your Amazon revenue is trending down and you need to protect profit without raising price or cutting ads.
steps: Track landed cost per unit separately from supplier price, including inbound freight.
Move as much volume as possible to sea freight when you have enough lead time; the source's landed cost fell from about $11 to about $7.50 per unit on the same product.
Pay the sample and blending or setup fees early to avoid expensive rush production later; the source paid roughly $400 for blend development and about $100 for a roughly 20-serving sample.
Reserve air freight for stockout emergencies and peak-season gaps only, since one unplanned air shipment cost over $60,000.
Recalculate margin after each cost change: in the source's month nine, profit was nearly $6,000 on about $14,000 revenue, higher margin than months with larger revenue.
caveats: Sea freight adds a six-week-or-more transit minimum, so it requires earlier inventory planning.
Landed-cost figures are from one product's case study.

cards.title: Analysis paralysis: launch timing matters more than a perfect supplier choice
cards.summary: Delaying a launch to perfect a decision costs more than the mistake you are avoiding, per the presenter's retrospective.
cards.use_when: You are stuck comparing suppliers, product ideas or listing details and delaying your first Amazon order.
steps: Quantify the cost of the delay: the presenter states that launching three months earlier would have earned roughly an extra $10,000 profit per month, about $30,000 in total.
Compare that cost to the worst plausible mistake, such as choosing a suboptimal manufacturer and paying $5,000 extra; the presenter argues the delay is the larger loss.
Set a decision deadline for supplier selection and place a first, small order rather than researching indefinitely.
Consider starting the business alongside existing employment, which the source says would have been far better than starting only after losing a job.
Reframe product ideas from a barrier to a routine: the source describes moving from not being able to generate ideas to seeing them everywhere once he had accumulated customer and topic knowledge.
caveats: The $10,000-per-month figure is one seller's retrospective estimate, not a forecast.
This advice applies to reversible decisions like a small first production run; large irreversible commitments deserve more diligence.

cards.title: Outsourcing the non-revenue tasks in an Amazon business
cards.summary: Delegate packing, editing and customer service so your time goes to the activities that actually drive sales.
cards.use_when: You are handling fulfillment, customer messages or video editing yourself and your marketing or sourcing work is slipping.
steps: Identify your revenue-driving activities; the source names social media and networking as his, and says these are hard to do while packing orders and editing video.
Hire out the mechanical work first: the source's example is packaging and shipping pre-orders (700+ units) by hand with friends and family before switching to FBA.
Use FBA for pick, pack and ship even when the fee feels high: the source paid over $7,700 in one month and called it worth every penny because it removed the labor and shipping cost.
Hire a video editor and customer service help as volume grows; the source notes this became necessary with a newborn and reduced his stress.
Recognize that 'passive income' in this model means the owner can step away once staff and FBA handle operations, not that the business runs without any input.
caveats: The source says fear of spending money delayed this hiring and slowed the business.
Outsourcing quality requires management attention; the source retained social media himself because he both enjoyed it and it was his main demand driver.

cards.title: Under-ordering inventory as the most expensive recurring mistake
cards.summary: Chronic under-ordering because of fear caps growth more than most other errors, per the source's own retrospective.
cards.use_when: You are deciding order quantity for your next Amazon production run while demand is trending up or a viral moment is in progress.
steps: Model the upside before choosing a quantity: the source estimates he lost roughly $300,000-$400,000 in sales from repeated and lengthy stockouts.
Consider that stockouts also suppress your own marketing, since the source says he stopped filming content in January partly because he had nothing to sell.
Size orders against realistic demand including viral potential, not just the last month's baseline; the source sold 200 units in two hours during one spike and had nothing left.
Accept that overstocking can be sold through wholesale, your own site and other marketplaces, while stockouts cannot be recovered for the lost demand window.
Review the balance with a mentor or advisor on a recurring cadence; the source and presenter met weekly and still repeatedly ordered too little.
caveats: Ordering too much carries real cash risk; the source had low bank balances after large orders and freight bills.
The $300,000-$400,000 figure is a retrospective estimate, not a measured counterfactual.

cards.title: Finding suppliers on Alibaba with trade assurance and verified filtering
cards.summary: Filter Alibaba to trade-assured, verified suppliers and review their operating history before contacting them.
cards.use_when: You are sourcing a product from overseas suppliers for your Amazon listing and need to screen manufacturers before paying anyone.
steps: Search Alibaba for your product, then enable the Trade Assurance and Verified Supplier filters, which restrict results to suppliers enrolled in Alibaba's payment protection and inspected by a third party.
Switch from the product view to the suppliers list to compare manufacturers directly rather than browsing product listings.
Screen each supplier on years in business, sales volume, staff size, rating and review count; the source treats a 4.9 rating with 200+ reviews as a strong signal.
Open the supplier profile to read their quality control process, production capacity and R&D capacity.
Contact suppliers through the platform and ask directly about customization, since the source notes suppliers often make items not shown on their Alibaba storefront.
Verify that current filter names and protections still work as described before relying on them, as marketplace interfaces change.
caveats: Verified and trade-assured status reduces but does not eliminate sourcing risk.
The source distinguishes suppliers (finished goods) from manufacturers (build from scratch); confirm which you are dealing with.

cards.title: Sourcing US-based manufacturers via Thomasnet, Google and phone calls
cards.summary: For products that need domestic manufacturing, use US directories and call rather than email to build a stronger connection.
cards.use_when: You need a domestic manufacturer for your product, for example when regulatory, safety or quality-control concerns make overseas production unattractive.
steps: Search Thomasnet for US suppliers; you can see location, founding year, employee count, capabilities and certifications after opening a profile.
Supplement with Google searches using the pattern '[product] manufacturers', '[product] private labelers' or '[product] suppliers'.

Call rather than email US manufacturers when possible: the source argues calling makes you seem more serious, lets you ask follow-up questions rapidly, and improves the chance they refer you to someone else if they can't help.
If a manufacturer can't produce your product, ask for a referral; phone conversations are more likely to produce one than email dead-ends.
Choose domestic production when the process involves something you can't verify overseas, such as precise caffeine dosing in the source's tea example, even though it costs more.
Verify directory names and interface details before use, as these sites change.
caveats: Domestic manufacturing typically costs more than overseas; the source accepted that trade-off for safety and communication reasons, and for low minimum order quantities.
The source's tea case involved a safety-sensitive additive, which strengthens the argument for domestic production more than it would for a simple commodity.

cards.title: Cold outreach at scale to find a manufacturer for a novel product
cards.summary: Blasting a clear, specific email to dozens of manufacturers across ten pages of search results is a workable way to find one willing to make an unusual product.
cards.use_when: You are sourcing a manufacturer for an unconventional product and most suppliers have said no or not replied.
steps: Open results from the first through roughly the tenth page of Google for manufacturer searches, then email each one individually through the contact address or form on their site.
Use the source's template components: what you are making, the specific technical requirement, a reference to an existing product that proves it can be done, and a request for a call.
Track who you contacted and their replies in a spreadsheet; the source contacted 50-60 manufacturers this way.
Write off non-responders unless the company looks like an ideal fit, in which case follow up; the source reasoned that non-responders likely wouldn't give good service anyway.

Use a dedicated email address for the campaign (the source used 'special blend 2000'), both to keep the resulting newsletters out of your personal inbox and to keep your outreach identity separate from your later phone identity.
If a domain-based address is available, use it for extra credibility, but a descriptive Gmail account is acceptable.
caveats: Expect many refusals, including claims that your product is impossible to make; the source found that most tea manufacturers said his caffeinated tea couldn't be done.
Using a separate email identity to gather information is described neutrally by the source but raises transparency questions.

cards.title: Questions to ask a manufacturer before committing
cards.summary: A short list of questions covering minimum order quantity, full cost structure, timeline and scope of work prevents surprises after you commit.
cards.use_when: You have found a manufacturer willing to produce your product and are preparing to place a first order.
steps: Ask for the minimum order quantity and any price breaks above it; the source's tea bags had an MOQ of 1,000 or 2,500 units with discounts at higher tiers.
Ask for all costs, not just the per-unit price; the source paid separately for blend development (about $400) and a sample (about $100 for roughly 20 servings).
Ask about the timeline for production and for each downstream step such as filling and packing.

Ask what they can and cannot do; the source's tea blender could blend and fill but not produce packaging, and referred him to a packaging house with low MOQs rather than leaving him to source it alone.
Ask about materials options that matter to your positioning, such as biodegradable stringless, tagless tea bags in the source case.
Accept a manufacturer's referral even if it costs more than sourcing overseas, when it keeps the process moving and gives you a dedicated account manager for artwork and printing issues.
caveats: A manufacturer's referral may not be the cheapest option; the source chose it for speed, communication and comfort, and notes that cost trade-offs should be judged per product.
Keep asking until you get a written confirmation of quantities and costs, since the source shows per-unit pricing alone understates total cost.

cards.title: Always ordering a physical sample before a production run
cards.summary: A paid sample validates product quality and taste before committing thousands to a production run.
cards.use_when: You have found a manufacturer and are about to place your first bulk order.
steps: Order a sample before production: the source paid about $100 for roughly 20 servings of tea plus about $400 in blending development.
Evaluate the sample yourself against the product spec, including whether the manufacturing process visibly worked as intended (the source could see the caffeine powder dusted on the leaves).
Get third-party expert feedback: the source took samples to coffee houses and tea shops in his town and used their tasting notes.
Test with friends and family for subjective reactions such as taste and perceived energy quality.
Only then place the production order; the source frames the sample as the check before spending thousands or tens of thousands.
caveats: A good sample does not guarantee consistent production quality at volume; the source separately valued the manufacturer's secrecy and control over their process.
Sample costs and lead times vary by product and manufacturer.

cards.title: Learning from refusals: phone calls as supplier education
cards.summary: Rejection calls are where manufacturers reveal why a product is hard to make and how it might be done, making you a more credible buyer next time.
cards.use_when: You are sourcing an unusual product and manufacturers keep declining; you want to convert those calls into useful technical intelligence.
steps: Take the call even when you expect a no; the source learned from one manufacturer that the only apparent route to a caffeinated loose-leaf product was spraying leaves with water and dusting caffeine powder, which risked mold and rot.
Record the technical constraints you hear and use them to refine your pitch to the next manufacturer.
Expect the phrase 'impossible' from established players; in the source's case, most traditional tea makers refused to alter their blends, but specialty blenders were open to a proprietary process.
Look for the segment of suppliers who already work on custom or specialty formulations, since those are the ones likely to attempt something unconventional.

Keep your product concept flexible in mechanism rather than outcome: the source considered alternatives such as a dissolving caffeine tablet in the tea bag while preserving the target of roughly 200 mg of caffeine per serving.
Verify any technical claim you hear on the phone in writing before committing money.
caveats: Supplier claims about feasibility may be wrong in either direction; the source's fear that every downstream step would be difficult proved unfounded once a partner was found.
A proprietary process you don't control creates dependency on that manufacturer.

cards.title: Finding competitors' manufacturers through Jungle Scout supplier lookups
cards.summary: Jungle Scout's supplier database can reveal the manufacturers behind existing Amazon products by company name or ASIN.
cards.use_when: You want a shortlist of vetted manufacturers already producing products similar to the one you plan to sell.
steps: Look up a competitor product on Amazon and note the brand or company name shown on the listing.
In Jungle Scout, open the Suppliers area and the supplier database, choose the company tab, and search the brand name to see its top suppliers.
Alternatively, copy the competitor's ASIN from the bottom of their listing page, then search the database by ASIN instead of company.
Use the results as a starting point for outreach, then screen each manufacturer the same way you would an Alibaba supplier.
Cross-check the result against the manufacturer's own site or a direct conversation before assuming the match is correct.
caveats: The source states this tool is not always 100% accurate but is accurate surprisingly often.
Tool menus and features change; verify the current interface before following these steps.
A competitor's manufacturer may be under contract or unable to take on a competing client.

cards.title: Using industry trade shows to build a manufacturer list
cards.summary: Trade show exhibitor lists for your product category are a ready-made roster of suppliers and manufacturers.
cards.use_when: You need a broad, category-specific supplier list and directories aren't producing enough candidates.
steps: Search Google for '[your product] conventions' or '[your product] trade show' to identify the main industry events.
Go to the event website and open the exhibitor list for the current or most recent year.
Work through the exhibitor list and contact each relevant company individually, treating it as a supplier outreach list.
If you can attend, walk the floor and talk to exhibitors directly, which the source recommends as faster and higher-signal than email.
Note that exhibitors at these events are typically suppliers and manufacturers rather than retailers.
caveats: The source treats attendance as optional; the exhibitor list alone is usable.
Exhibitor lists can be long and include non-manufacturing companies; budget time for triage.

cards.title: Sourcing European manufacturers for a non-US seller
cards.summary: Directory sites such as Europages help sellers based outside the US find manufacturers in their own region.
cards.use_when: Your business is based in the UK or Europe and you want a local manufacturer for lead times, communication or regulatory reasons.
steps: Search Europages for your product category to produce a list of UK or European manufacturers.
Screen each result on the same criteria you would use on Alibaba or Thomasnet: years established, size, capabilities and certifications.
Call local manufacturers where possible, since the source argues phone contact creates a stronger impression and yields referrals.
Prefer regional manufacturing when it shortens the iteration cycle on samples and packaging artwork; the source valued having a reachable contact for artwork and color decisions.
Verify the directory site is still current and covers your country before relying on it.
caveats: The source lists Europages as a starting point without comparing it to other European directories.
Regional manufacturing usually costs more than overseas sourcing; the source accepted that for ease and safety on a sensitive product.

cards.title: Assuming one manufacturer won't do everything
cards.summary: Specialist manufacturers often handle only their core step, so plan for a second supplier for packaging or finishing.
cards.use_when: You are mapping your production process and budgeting for how many suppliers and handoffs you need.
steps: Ask your primary manufacturer explicitly what their scope of work covers before assuming they are a one-stop shop.
Expect gaps: in the source's case the blender produced the tea but not the packaging, and the tea sat in a warehouse waiting for packaging to arrive from a separate manufacturer.
Ask for referrals to fill the gap; the source's blender recommended a US packaging house with low minimum order quantities.

Decide whether to accept a referral at a higher cost versus sourcing independently for less: the source chose the referral to keep the process moving and to get a dedicated account manager for design files and print considerations.
Account for the extra lead time created by multiple suppliers in your launch and restock planning.
caveats: Multi-supplier setups add coordination overhead and more points of failure.
The source's choice of a more expensive domestic packaging supplier was specific to his artwork complexity and low MOQ needs.
